werk/gil-evans-paris-blues.text:
Paris Blues is a duo album by the pianist Gil Evans and the saxophonist Steve Lacy, recorded in Paris in 1987 and released on the French label Owl. It was Evans's last studio recording before his death in 1988. In the United States it did not appear until 2003, on Sunnyside Records.

Evans plays piano and electric piano, Lacy soprano saxophone. The repertoire consists of pieces by Charles Mingus, such as Reincarnation of a Lovebird and Goodbye Pork Pie Hat, Duke Ellington's Paris Blues and Lacy's own Esteem. The longest piece lasts almost fifteen minutes. The reviews were moderate. Scott Yanow felt that the pianist mostly prompted and accompanied with melodies, and The Penguin Guide to Jazz called the result light and agreeable.
werk/gil-evans-paris-blues.listen: Listen to Duke Ellington's Paris Blues and notice how piano and soprano saxophone respond to each other in a duet.

werk/gil-evans-the-individualism-of-gil-.text:
The Individualism of Gil Evans was released in 1964 on Verve and presents the pianist and arranger Gil Evans at the head of a big band. The recordings were made in New York and Englewood Cliffs, spread over 1963 and 1964. The programme consists of five originals, two of them co-written with Miles Davis, and compositions by Kurt Weill, Bob Dorough, John Lewis and Willie Dixon.

The original LP contained four pieces. The 1988 CD added five more, including Willie Dixon's Spoonful. The album earned a Grammy nomination. AllMusic gave it four stars out of five and regretted that the arranger did not record more in this period.
werk/gil-evans-the-individualism-of-gil-.listen: Listen to Kurt Weill's The Barbara Song and notice how an existing composition is worked out here as a big band piece.

werk/gilbert-o-sullivan-a-stranger-in-my.text:
After the funk-flavoured predecessor I'm a Writer, Not a Fighter, Gilbert O'Sullivan returned on his fourth album to the style of his first two records. He wrote the songs in early 1974 during two months in a small fishing village in Portugal. Gordon Mills produced again and Johnnie Spence made the arrangements. For the first time he did not record at Audio International Studios in London, but at two American studios, in New York and Los Angeles.

A Woman's Place became the only single. Some saw the lyrics as sexist, and the song received little airplay. My Father, I Wonder Would You Mind and Always Somebody are sparse: just O'Sullivan at the piano, with a single horn solo in My Father. The record was released in October 1974 in an elaborate sleeve resembling a bound book and reached number 9 on the British albums chart. It was his last top 10 album.
werk/gilbert-o-sullivan-a-stranger-in-my.listen: Listen to My Father and notice how little is needed: the piano, the voice and a single horn solo.

werk/gilbert-o-sullivan-back-to-front.text:
Back to Front is Gilbert O'Sullivan's second album and was released in October 1972 on MAM Records. It followed the debut Himself and the worldwide hit Alone Again (Naturally). The singer wrote the songs at home in nocturnal sessions and recorded them with Gordon Mills at Audio International Studios in London, again with the arranger Johnnie Spence. Mills had most of the vocals double-tracked. At the same time his image changed: the cap and short trousers gave way to a perm and sweaters with a G on them.

The record combines pop in the showbiz tradition with strings, but contains more piano songs than before. Clair is about babysitting Mills's daughter and became a number 1 in the United Kingdom. In But I'm Not you can hear the influence of Fats Domino. The album reached the top of the British chart and was well received by critics.
werk/gilbert-o-sullivan-back-to-front.listen: Listen to Clair and notice how the singer tells, almost as in a train of thought, about babysitting his producer's little daughter.

werk/gilbert-o-sullivan-himself.text:
Himself is the debut of the Irish singer and songwriter Gilbert O'Sullivan and was released in August 1971 on MAM Records, after the hit Nothing Rhymed. The producer and manager Gordon Mills recorded the album at Audio International Studios in London. The singer wanted only to sing and play piano, but Mills persuaded him to have full accompaniment with arrangements by Johnnie Spence.

The songs are observant and conversational, with wordplay in which he sees the influence of Spike Milligan. Permissive Twit tells of a girl with an unwanted pregnancy, Houdini Said is about young people rioting, and Thunder and Lightning is one of the brightest numbers. The album begins and ends with a short intro and outro. It reached number 5 on the British albums chart and was well received. His cap and short trousers also drew attention.
werk/gilbert-o-sullivan-himself.listen: Listen to Nothing Rhymed and notice the wordplay in the lyrics, such as Bonaparte shandy instead of Napoléon brandy.

werk/gilbert-o-sullivan-i-m-a-writer-not.text:
After 1972, when he was one of the most successful artists in the world, Gilbert O'Sullivan sought new directions on his third album. He recorded the record on and off in 1973 in the new studio of his manager and producer Gordon Mills, next to Mills's house. Mills played keyboards and sang backing vocals, and Johnnie Spence again made the string arrangements. O'Sullivan himself called it a very ad hoc project, made at home.

The music leans on rock and funk, with electric keyboards and under the influence of Stevie Wonder. Unlike earlier records, the album does not open with a short intro piece, but with the title song, which combines blues and soul. Get Down had been a number 1 in the United Kingdom months earlier. Ooh Baby did not make the British top 10. The album reached number 2 on the British albums chart. Critics were divided, but the verdict has become more favourable over time.
werk/gilbert-o-sullivan-i-m-a-writer-not.listen: Listen to Not In a Million Years and notice how reggae and rumba run into each other, with unexpected harmonies.

werk/giorgio-moroder-son-of-my-father.text:
Son of My Father, from 1972, is an album that Giorgio Moroder composed, produced and performed himself. He recorded it at his own Musicland Studios, together with Pete Bellotte as coordinator and musicians such as the drummer Keith Forsey. Moroder played guitar and synthesizers and also used a Moog.

Three pieces, Tears, Underdog and Son of My Father, were heard in the film Die Klosterschülerinnen, for which Moroder also wrote the music. Automation was heard in the film Oswalt Kolle: Liebe als Gesellschaftsspiel. The title song became better known still in the version by the English group Chicory Tip. Tears also continued to resonate: the group Shirocco later made a version with vocals of it, under the title Es War Nur Ein Traum.
werk/giorgio-moroder-son-of-my-father.listen: Listen to Son Of My Father and notice the synthesizer: hear how an electronic sound plays the leading role here in a pop song.

werk/gladys-knight-en-the-pips-everybody.text:
Everybody Needs Love is the third studio album by Gladys Knight & the Pips and their first for Motown's Soul label. The producer Norman Whitfield made most of it. The album contains four singles: Just Walk in My Shoes, their Motown debut in 1966, Take Me in Your Arms and Love Me, Everybody Needs Love and I Heard It Through the Grapevine.

Everybody Needs Love reached number 39 on the Billboard Hot 100 and was their first big hit for the label. I Heard It Through the Grapevine did far better, reaching number two. It then became the best-selling single in Motown's history. Its success was later overshadowed by the version by Marvin Gaye, which appeared a year afterwards on the Tamla label.
werk/gladys-knight-en-the-pips-everybody.listen: In I Heard It Through the Grapevine, listen to the rhythm and Gladys Knight's vocals, and compare it with the version by Marvin Gaye.

werk/golden-earring-eight-miles-high.text:
This fifth studio album came out in 1969 on Polydor in Europe and on Atlantic in the United States. It was the first album under the name The Golden Earring, previously Golden Earrings, and the only one with the drummer Sieb Warner.

The record has only five pieces. Barry Hay sings tracks 1, 2 and 4, George Kooymans tracks 3 and 5. Hay also plays flute on Song of a Devil's Servant. Rinus Gerritsen plays bass, organ and piano. In the United States an edited version of Eight Miles High was released as a single, without the band's permission; in Europe no singles came from the album.
werk/golden-earring-eight-miles-high.listen: In Song of a Devil's Servant, listen to Barry Hay's flute in the band.

werk/golden-earring-moontan.text:
Moontan is the ninth studio album by the Dutch rock band Golden Earring and came out in August 1973 on Polydor, in England on Track Records and in the United States on MCA. The band produced it themselves, with Fred Haayen as executive producer. The album was mixed at IBC Studios in London. On Radar Love, the radio hit of the album, Eelco Gelling plays slide guitar. In Vanilla Queen, two lines by Marilyn Monroe from the film There's No Business Like Show Business are sampled.

In the United States Moontan became the group's most successful album. It is the only Golden Earring album to go gold there, certified by the RIAA. The American edition first appeared with the English sleeve of an exotic dancer, but that was soon replaced by the sleeve with the earring.
werk/golden-earring-moontan.listen: In Radar Love, listen to Eelco Gelling's slide guitar.

werk/golden-earring-on-the-double.text:
This fourth studio album by Golden Earrings was their first double album and came out in 1969 on Polydor. It was the last album under the name Golden Earrings and the last with the drummer Jaap Eggermont, who wanted to become a producer and later made Stars on 45. Fred Haayen produced the record.

The record has many styles side by side: psychedelic rock in Song of a Devil's Servant, baroque pop and orchestral ballads in Angelina and Just a Little Bit of Peace in My Heart, acoustic folk in Judy and Murdock 9-6182, and hard rock in Backbiting Baby. In November 2025 a remastered reissue appeared from the original master tapes, with the two stand-alone singles of that period as extras.
werk/golden-earring-on-the-double.listen: In Song of a Devil's Servant, listen to the band's psychedelic sound, the beginning of a long, varied record.

werk/golden-earring-radar-love.text: In 1973 Radar Love by Golden Earring from The Hague was released, a rock song about a man driving to his lover at night. It became a hit in England and America and is one of the best-known rock songs for the car. Golden Earring existed from 1961 to 2021, one of the longest-running rock bands in the world. The band stopped when the guitarist George Kooymans was diagnosed with ALS.
werk/golden-earring-radar-love.listen: The bass and the drums hit the motorway: the groove is the song. Also listen for the drum solo in the middle.

werk/golden-earring-seven-tears.text:
Seven Tears is the seventh studio album by the Dutch rock band Golden Earring and was released in 1971 on Polydor. The record was not released in the United States. Fred Haayen produced the album, and Albert Kos and Pieter Nieboer recorded it. The four band members were helped by the saxophonist Bertus Borgers, who plays on two pieces. The singer Barry Hay also plays flute, while Rinus Gerritsen plays organ, piano and an ARP synthesizer as well as bass.

She Flies On Strange Wings was released from the record as a single. The band did not want to shorten the album version of just over seven minutes. They therefore cut the song in two at 4:31 and released it as Part 1 and Part 2, spread over the two sides of the single.
werk/golden-earring-seven-tears.listen: Listen to She Flies On Strange Wings and notice which instruments can be heard besides guitar and drums in this long piece.

werk/gorillaz-demon-days.text:
This second album by the virtual band was made at Studio 13 in London, mainly under the direction of the producer Danger Mouse. A film plan for the band was scrapped, but themes from the script remained. The main inspiration came from a train journey from Beijing to Mongolia, in which Damon Albarn travelled through a deserted, withered region of China. He saw the album as a loose concept record about a world in a state of night, with apocalyptic and post-9/11 themes. It is darker than the debut.

The music mixes alternative rock, hip hop, pop, trip hop and art rock. Guests included De La Soul, Neneh Cherry, Martina Topley-Bird, MF Doom, Ike Turner and Dennis Hopper. Feel Good Inc. became the best-known single and won the band its only Grammy. The reviews were positive and showed that the project was more than a side step. Later the album grew into one of the most highly regarded records of the century.
werk/gorillaz-demon-days.listen: Listen to Feel Good Inc., the first single, and notice how dark and menacing the atmosphere is for a big hit.

werk/grace-jones-muse.text:
Muse was released on 4 September 1979 on Island Records. It is Grace Jones's third album and the last of her disco trilogy with the producer Tom Moulton, which began in 1977 with Portfolio. As on the previous records, the first side is a continuous medley of four songs, linked by a story about someone who has sinned. The second side consists of separate disco songs. The Icelandic keyboard player Thor Baldursson, who did most of the arranging and sings a duet with her on Suffer, had earlier worked in Munich with, among others, Donna Summer and Giorgio Moroder.

The record came out in the year of the anti-disco backlash. The album and the only single, On Your Knees, were largely ignored, and Muse is regarded as her lost album. Billboard called the music, vocals and production top-notch, and Cash Box praised the sophisto-disco sound and Baldursson's band. The Quietus later called it the best of her first three records.
werk/grace-jones-muse.listen: Listen to Suffer and hear how her voice and Thor Baldursson's sound together.

werk/grace-jones-portfolio.text:
Portfolio is the debut album of the Jamaican singer Grace Jones, released in 1977 on Island Records. Earlier she had worked as a model in Paris and New York and had released a few singles in 1975 and 1976 without a breakthrough. The album was recorded and mixed at Sigma Sound Studios in Philadelphia, with the disco producer Tom Moulton, with whom she made three albums.

The first side of the LP is a continuous disco medley of three songs from Broadway musicals: Send in the Clowns, What I Did for Love and Tomorrow. Side two opens with her own performance of Édith Piaf's La Vie en rose, which became her first big hit and reached the top five in France and Italy. Sorry and That's the Trouble were her first own songs. I Need a Man became a number one dance hit in the United States. The reviews were mixed: Billboard thought it perfect to dance to, while AllMusic called it more a producer's record.
werk/grace-jones-portfolio.listen: Listen to the medley on the first side and notice how the songs from the musicals run into one another without a break, in disco style.

werk/graham-coxon-the-golden-d.text:
Two years after his first solo record, Graham Coxon made a second album in 2000, which stood further from Blur than his debut. He recorded all the instruments himself, and also produced and mixed the record himself. The guitars and the vocals sound heavier and even rawer than before. Only Keep Hope Alive resembles the sound of The Sky Is Too High. There are two covers on it, Fame and Fortune and That's When I Reach for My Revolver, both by the post-punk band Mission of Burma. The title is a joke about Coxon's favourite guitar chord.

Reactions were mixed. A reviewer at AllMusic heard mainly hard and fast rock and thought of Sonic Youth and the Sex Pistols. The sleeve shows part of Coxon's own painting The Blue Dog.
werk/graham-coxon-the-golden-d.listen: Listen to Fame and Fortune and notice how raw the guitars and vocals sound. This song is a cover of Mission of Burma.

werk/graham-coxon-the-kiss-of-morning.text:
The Kiss of Morning is the fourth solo album by Graham Coxon, guitarist of Blur. It was released on 21 October 2002 in the United Kingdom and was his first record since he had left Blur for the first time. The title stems from his changed outlook on life after he struggled with alcoholism and became sober. He wrote all the songs himself.

In its execution, too, it is a personal work. Coxon plays guitars, bass, drums, harmonica and percussion, sings, produced together with Mike Pelanconi and even painted the sleeve. Louis Vause adds piano, Fender Rhodes and Hammond, B.J. Cole pedal steel. The song All I Wanna Do Iz Listen to Yuz appeared in 2004 as the B-side of Bittersweet Bundle of Misery.
werk/graham-coxon-the-kiss-of-morning.listen: Listen to Latte, on which B.J. Cole plays, and notice how the pedal steel relates to the guitar.

werk/graham-coxon-the-sky-is-too-high.text:
In August 1998, Graham Coxon, guitarist of Blur, released his first solo album on his own label Transcopic Records. He wrote, recorded and produced all the music himself. Most of it consists of acoustic songs with a lo-fi sound, here and there supplemented with electric guitar and drums. In this way the record resembles Blur songs such as Miss America and You're So Great, one of the few songs on which Coxon himself sings.

The Guardian felt that the album could not match the work of Syd Barrett, but praised Coxon's gift for playing in a way that is messy and yet attractive. On the sleeve there is still a crossed-out track titled pause, but it is not on the record: there are eleven tracks.
werk/graham-coxon-the-sky-is-too-high.listen: Listen to Mornin' Blues and notice how simple and homely it sounds, in keeping with the lo-fi character of the record.

werk/gram-parsons-grievous-angel.text:
After a disorganised tour in the spring and summer of 1973, Gram Parsons recorded his second solo album at Wally Heider Studio 4 in Hollywood, with himself as producer. His singing partner Emmylou Harris and members of Elvis Presley's band, including James Burton and Glen Hardin, played on it. Parsons struggled with heroin and alcohol, but according to the bassist Emory Gordy the sessions were loose and full of energy. Because there was too little new material, he wrote two songs during the recording and used older songs. Shortly after the mixing he died of an overdose.

The record came out in January 1974. It is a blend of country and rock 'n' roll that he called Cosmic American Music. In the duet Love Hurts, Harris has a large role. The album sold poorly, but critics were full of praise. His widow had Harris removed from the front of the sleeve and had one song left off.
werk/gram-parsons-grievous-angel.listen: In Love Hurts, listen to the two voices of Parsons and Emmylou Harris and how they find each other in the chorus.

werk/grandmaster-flash-ba-dop-boom-bang.text:
Ba-Dop-Boom-Bang is Grandmaster Flash's fifth album and was released in 1987 on Elektra. The cassette version was called Ba-Dop-Boom-Bang...And More and the CD Ba-Dop-Boom-Bang...And Even More, both with extra tracks that were not on the original vinyl record. The record opens with a short version of Ain't We Funkin' Now and closes with a reprise of it. In between are, among others, U Know What Time It Is, Kid Named Flash, Tear the Roof Off and I Am Somebody.

On European pressings the title of All Wrapped Up was misprinted as All Rapped Up. In 2005 the record was reissued on CD by Collectors' Choice Music, with the original track listing of the vinyl record without extra tracks. The booklet contained a new essay by Peter Relic.
werk/grandmaster-flash-ba-dop-boom-bang.listen: Listen to the short Ain't We Funkin' Now that opens the album and also closes it in a reprise. Can you hear how the opening track returns?

werk/grandmaster-flash-the-bridge-concep.text:
The Bridge (Concept of a Culture) is Grandmaster Flash's seventh studio album, released on 24 February 2009 on Strut Records. It was his first studio album since Flash Is Back in 1998. Flash himself handled most of the production. Three CD versions appeared: a clean and an explicit standard edition with 19 tracks, and a bonus edition with two exclusive remixes. In addition, a double vinyl record came out in the United States.

The album features many guests from hip hop, among them Q-Tip, Busta Rhymes, Snoop Dogg, Big Daddy Kane, MC Supernatural, Grandmaster Caz, Afasi and Kase-O. In this way generations and countries come together on one record. Shine All Day, with Q-Tip, Kel Spencer and Jumz, also appeared in a remix by Sam Webster as a bonus track.
werk/grandmaster-flash-the-bridge-concep.listen: Listen to Shine All Day and notice the voice of Q-Tip, one of the guests on this album.

werk/grateful-dead-american-beauty.text:
This album came out in November 1970, shortly after Workingman's Dead, and continued the folk and country of that album. The songwriters Jerry Garcia and Robert Hunter were in a fertile period, and now other band members wrote as well: Phil Lesh with Box of Rain, Bob Weir with Sugar Magnolia and Pigpen with Operator. The recording began shortly after it emerged that the manager Lenny Hart had renewed the contract with Warner without the group's knowledge and had disappeared with a good part of the money. The studio engineer Stephen Barncard took over the production from Bob Matthews.

Garcia played less lead guitar and more pedal steel. The mandolin player David Grisman plays on Friend of the Devil and above all on Ripple. The sound is mainly acoustic, with major-key melodies and folk harmonies, under the influence of Dylan and the studio neighbours Crosby, Stills, Nash & Young. Rolling Stone placed the album at number 258 of the 500 best albums in 2003.
werk/grateful-dead-american-beauty.listen: Listen to Ripple and notice David Grisman's mandolin, which together with the acoustic guitars and the harmony singing shapes the atmosphere of the song.

werk/grateful-dead-anthem-of-the-sun.text:
Anthem of the Sun, the second album by the Grateful Dead, was released on 18 July 1968. The recording began in late 1967 in Los Angeles with the producer David Hassinger and moved to New York. Hassinger dropped out, because the group worked too slowly and too experimentally. Back in San Francisco the members also recorded their concerts. Jerry Garcia, Phil Lesh and the sound engineer Dan Healy spliced those live recordings together with studio tracks into a new whole. In this way an album came about that is neither a pure studio album nor a live record.

The group also used, among other things, prepared piano, harpsichord, kazoo and timpani. Tom Constanten brought ideas from John Cage and Karlheinz Stockhausen. It was the first album with the second drummer Mickey Hart. Warner Bros. called the project the most unreasonable thing the company had ever done. Rolling Stone later included it in its list of the five hundred best albums.
werk/grateful-dead-anthem-of-the-sun.listen: Listen to Alligator and notice the jam section after the vocals. That part comes from a live performance and was attached to the studio recording.

werk/grateful-dead-aoxomoxoa.text:
This third studio album by the Grateful Dead came out in 1969 and was recorded twice. The first version, with the working title Earthquake Country, went in the bin when Ampex released the first 16-track recorder. The band spent eight months in the studio, partly to experiment with the new technology, and that cost a fortune. It was also the first album on which the lyricist Robert Hunter took part fully, alongside Jerry Garcia. For the first time an acoustic side of the band was heard, for example in Mountains of the Moon and Dupree's Diamond Blues. Garcia sang lead on every track.

The result is psychedelic rock full of overdubs, choirs and electronic sounds. Of the songs, only China Cat Sunflower remained a staple on the stage. Rolling Stone wrote enthusiastically about the music in 1969. In 1971 Garcia and Lesh remixed the album, in which much of the experimental material disappeared.
werk/grateful-dead-aoxomoxoa.listen: Listen to Mountains of the Moon and notice how acoustic and restrained the band sounds here, very different from the long live improvisations.

werk/grateful-dead-from-the-mars-hotel.text:
From the Mars Hotel was recorded mainly in April 1974 and was released on 27 June of that year, less than a year after Wake of the Flood. It was the second record on the Grateful Dead's own label and the last before a long break from touring. The band chose Coast Recorders in San Francisco and produced it themselves, with the engineer Roy Segal. Jerry Garcia found the room sounded livelier than the Record Plant.

Most of the songs came from Garcia and the lyricist Robert Hunter. Phil Lesh sang Unbroken Chain and Pride of Cucamonga, his last lead vocals for the band until 1985. Scarlet Begonias had appeared only a month earlier and later became a highlight of the concerts. U.S. Blues came out as a single. The sleeve shows a real building in San Francisco in an extraterrestrial landscape. Christgau called the album more cheerful than its predecessor, with almost as many memorable melodies as American Beauty.
werk/grateful-dead-from-the-mars-hotel.listen: Listen to Unbroken Chain and notice Ned Lagin's synthesizer and Phil Lesh, who takes the lead vocal himself.

werk/grateful-dead-wake-of-the-flood.text:
Wake of the Flood was released on 15 October 1973 as the first album on the Grateful Dead's own label. It was their first studio record in almost three years and the first without Ron McKernan, nicknamed Pigpen, who had died shortly before. New were the keyboard player Keith Godchaux and his wife Donna Jean, a singer. His preference for bebop and modal jazz gave the music a different direction from Pigpen's blues.

The band recorded the album between 4 and 15 August 1973 at the Record Plant in Sausalito. The songs had been tried out live for months. They mix country, folk, R&B, ragtime and jazz rock. Row Jimmy has a slow tempo with a light reggae groove, and Weather Report Suite by Bob Weir is the grand finale. The title comes from the first lines of Here Comes Sunshine. The album climbed higher in the pop charts than American Beauty: number 18.
werk/grateful-dead-wake-of-the-flood.listen: Listen to Row Jimmy and try to hear how the slow tempo goes together with a light reggae groove underneath.

werk/green-day-american-idiot.text:
After the disappointing Warning of 2000, the members of Green Day stood at a crossroads. They were quarrelling and wanted a new direction. A first album, Cigarettes and Valentines, vanished when the master tapes were stolen. The producer Rob Cavallo helped the band to start again. From short fragments of thirty seconds grew suites such as Homecoming and Jesus of Suburbia. In this way American Idiot, released on 21 September 2004, became a punk rock opera about a boy from the American middle class.

The record was made in Oakland and Los Angeles and took ten months. The band listened to rock operas such as Tommy and Quadrophenia by The Who. Besides punk, new wave, Latin and polka can be heard. The title song is about the politics of those years, after 9/11 and the war in Iraq. Boulevard of Broken Dreams won a Grammy for Record of the Year. The album reached number 1 on the American chart, won a Grammy for Best Rock Album and inspired a Broadway musical.
werk/green-day-american-idiot.listen: Listen to Jesus of Suburbia and notice how the song is built from separate parts, like chapters of a story.

werk/green-day-dookie.text:
Green Day had made two albums for the independent Lookout! Records when major labels came knocking. The band chose Reprise because the producer Rob Cavallo understood them well, and signed in April 1993. Dookie was recorded that year at Fantasy Studios in Berkeley and Music Grinder Studio in Hollywood. For the first time the band members had ample time and money to perfect sounds and guitar tones. Many old fans afterwards called the band sellouts.

Billie Joe Armstrong wrote most of the songs, about boredom, anxiety, relationships and sexuality. After years of grunge, the album brought a livelier and more melodic rock sound to the general public. Singles were Longview, Basket Case, Welcome to Paradise in a new version and When I Come Around. The album received glowing reviews and a Grammy for Best Alternative Album. It is regarded as a model for later punk and pop punk bands.
werk/green-day-dookie.listen: In Longview, listen to the melody and the way the lyrics describe boredom. Notice how melodic the band sounds, despite the fast tempo.

werk/green-day-insomniac.text:
Insomniac was released on 10 October 1995 on Reprise Records, as the successor to the breakthrough record Dookie. The band recorded the album at Hyde Street in San Francisco and opted for energetic takes. Success had also earned Green Day distrust in the punk world. Billie Joe Armstrong was branded a sellout, and the group wanted to prove that they belonged.

The sound is heavier and harder than on Dookie, and the lyrics are gloomier. They are about alienation, anxiety, boredom and drug use. Panic Song begins with a pounding intro of almost two minutes, during which the drummer Tré Cool tore the skin off his hands. Brain Stew and Jaded follow each other directly. 86 is about the rejection by the Gilman Street club in Berkeley. The reviews were mostly positive and praised the lyrics and the sarcastic humour.
werk/green-day-insomniac.listen: Listen to Panic Song and notice the pounding instrumental intro, which lasts two minutes before the vocals begin. Hear how the drumming drives the song forward.

werk/green-day-nimrod.text:
After Insomniac, which was less successful than Dookie, Green Day decided in 1996 to cancel the European tour. The group had had enough of playing in large arenas and missed home. In that time the band wrote more than thirty new songs. Rob Cavallo remained producer and the recording at Conway Recording Studios in Los Angeles took four months. Billie Joe Armstrong wanted to break through the limitations of ordinary punk rock, with London Calling by the Clash as inspiration.

The album therefore sounds varied: folk, hardcore, surf rock and ska stand side by side. Hitchin' a Ride opens with a violin, King for a Day has a horn section and Good Riddance (Time of Your Life) was given strings. That last song was heard, among other places, in Seinfeld. The reviews were favourable and praised the songwriting in particular.
werk/green-day-nimrod.listen: Listen to Good Riddance (Time of Your Life) and notice how an acoustic guitar and strings take the place of the usual punk guitars.

werk/green-day-warning.text:
Warning was released on 3 October 2000 and is Green Day's sixth studio album. The band first worked with the producer Scott Litt, but they differed in opinion on the musical direction. Rob Cavallo then returned as executive producer, while the band themselves did most of the production work. The recording took place at Studio 880 in Oakland. While writing, Billie Joe Armstrong listened a lot to Bob Dylan's Bringing It All Back Home.

The album largely leaves behind the usual punk sound and uses more acoustic guitars, pop and folk. Misery has mariachi horns, strings and accordion; Waiting is based on a riff from Downtown by Petula Clark. The lyrics are more optimistic and sometimes political, as in Minority. The reviews were mostly positive, but commercially the album was a disappointment.
werk/green-day-warning.listen: Listen to Misery and notice the horns, strings and accordion alongside the guitar. Also follow how the stories in the verses all end badly.

werk/grover-washington-jr-all-the-king-s.text:
This second album by Grover Washington Jr. was recorded in 1972 and came out the same year on Kudu. It was produced by Creed Taylor, with recording by Rudy Van Gelder and arrangements by Bob James, who plays electric piano and harpsichord. A large ensemble with brass and strings stands behind the saxophonist.

The record has pop songs and standards. The title song comes from Aretha Franklin, Lean on Me from Bill Withers, Lover Man is a jazz standard and Love Song 1700 is based on Henry Purcell. There is solo work by guitarists such as Eric Gale and David Spinozza. In 2008 the record was reissued on CD by Verve and GRP.
werk/grover-washington-jr-all-the-king-s.listen: In Lean On Me, listen to how the saxophone sings Withers's melody.

werk/grover-washington-jr-feels-so-good.text:
Feels So Good is the fifth album by the saxophonist Grover Washington Jr. and was recorded and released in 1975. The producer Creed Taylor worked with the arranger Bob James, who provided the spacious, rich sonic setting. Rudy Van Gelder was the engineer. The record has five pieces, with strings, brass and a strong rhythm section.

The album topped both the soul and the jazz chart and reached tenth place on the pop albums chart. The reviewer Jason Ankeny later called it the creative high point of Washington's electric funk sound. According to him, the record shows that smooth jazz is more than background music. He also lauded the bassist Louis Johnson, who in It Feels So Good and Hydra drives the bottom end of the music while the soprano sax floats above.
werk/grover-washington-jr-feels-so-good.listen: Listen to It Feels So Good and notice how the bass carries the groove while the soprano sax solos above it.

werk/grover-washington-jr-inner-city-blu.text:
Grover Washington Jr. made his debut with this album, recorded in September 1971 at the Van Gelder Studio and released in 1972 on Kudu. Creed Taylor produced, and Bob James wrote the arrangements and conducted. Ron Carter, Eric Gale and Idris Muhammad, among others, also play.

The title song is a cover of Marvin Gaye's recent hit of June 1971. Bill Withers's Ain't No Sunshine, released shortly before, is also on the record, alongside Mercy Mercy Me, Georgia on My Mind and I Loves You Porgy. Thom Jurek of AllMusic called it a stunning debut and a milestone and turning point in jazz. A series of albums for the label followed until the end of the 1970s.
werk/grover-washington-jr-inner-city-blu.listen: In Inner City Blues, listen to how the saxophone takes over Gaye's melody.

werk/grover-washington-jr-mister-magic.text:
Mister Magic is the fourth album by the saxophonist Grover Washington Jr. and came out in February 1975. Creed Taylor produced, Rudy Van Gelder recorded it, and Bob James wrote the arrangements and played piano and Fender Rhodes. Washington plays soprano, alto and tenor saxophone. An orchestra of strings and brass fills out the sound. The record contains four pieces.

The album topped both the soul and the jazz chart and reached tenth place on the pop albums chart. The critics were divided. Robert Christgau found it functional and praised the danceably bubbling rhythm section, but found the strings intrusive. Scott Yanow later called it a much-loved work and a classic of R&B-tinged jazz, with colourful arrangements that are somewhat commercial.
werk/grover-washington-jr-mister-magic.listen: Listen to Mister Magic and notice how the rhythm section provides the danceable groove, with the saxophone above it.

werk/gucci-mane-hard-to-kill.text:
Hard to Kill is Gucci Mane's second studio album, released on 24 October 2006 through Big Cat Records and Tommy Boy Records. Most of the beats came from Zaytoven. Four tracks were made by others, including Cyber Sapp, Nitti, Josh Butler, Chead George and Paul Roach. Guests on the record include Black Magic, Mac Bre-Z, Gangsta Boo, La Chat and Young Snead.

The first single, My Chain, came out in June 2006, and Freaky Girl followed as the second. The reviews were mixed. A reviewer at XXL felt that the guests break the monotony, but still called it a heavy listen.
werk/gucci-mane-hard-to-kill.listen: In My Chain, the album's first single, listen to Zaytoven's beat.

werk/gucci-mane-the-appeal-georgia-s-mos.text:
Gucci Mane spent twelve months in the Fulton County Jail in Georgia in 2009 and 2010. After his release he put out a stream of mixtapes, songs and videos in May 2010 and named his label 1017 Brick Squad Records. The Appeal: Georgia's Most Wanted is a follow-up to The State vs. Radric Davis from 2009 and was released on 28 September 2010.

Besides his regular producers, including Zaytoven, Shawty Redd and Drumma Boy, he worked for the first time with Swizz Beatz, Wyclef Jean and Pharrell Williams. By his own account he made six tracks with Swizz and six with Pharrell, and picked the best from those. He considered the album his best representation of where he stood musically and mentally. It entered at number four on the Billboard 200.
werk/gucci-mane-the-appeal-georgia-s-mos.listen: Listen to Haterade. Notice how Nicki Minaj and Pharrell Williams share the song with the rapper.

werk/gucci-mane-trap-house.text:
Trap House is the debut album of the American rapper Gucci Mane. It came out on 24 May 2005 on Big Cat Records and Tommy Boy Records. The beats came from, among others, Shawty Redd, Zaytoven, Nitti and The Heatmakerz, and many guests take part, among them Young Jeezy, Killer Mike, Lil Scrappy and Bun B.

Five singles supported the record: Icy, Go Head, Money Don't Matter, the title track Trap House and That's All. Icy was the first, with Young Jeezy and Boo, produced by Zaytoven. Go Head also appears on the next album. In the United States, Trap House entered at number 101 on the Billboard 200 and reached number five on the independent albums chart.
werk/gucci-mane-trap-house.listen: In Icy, listen to how Gucci Mane, Young Jeezy and Boo alternate over a beat by Zaytoven.

werk/guided-by-voices-alien-lanes.text:
Alien Lanes was released in April 1995 and was Guided by Voices' first album for Matador Records. The advances were high, almost a hundred thousand dollars, one of the most expensive deals in the label's history. The recording, by contrast, cost about ten dollars, not counting the beer. The record has twenty-eight short songs, often only a minute or two long.

Rolling Stone called the music catchy rock with a sometimes prickly, sometimes playful urge to experiment. The Guardian found the songs gems that stop just short of being too idiosyncratic. AllMusic heard a record similar to Bee Thousand, with fewer obvious masterpieces but also fewer flaws. Pitchfork placed it at number 27 among the best albums of the 1990s, and Magnet proclaimed it the best album of 1995.
werk/guided-by-voices-alien-lanes.listen: Listen to Cigarette Tricks, which lasts less than twenty seconds, and notice how much happens in such a short time.

werk/guided-by-voices-bee-thousand.text:
Guided by Voices from Dayton, Ohio, was not a band in the usual sense: whichever of a group of friends had time played along. In 1993 Robert Pollard was on the point of disbanding the group, because of lack of money and because he wanted to look after his family and his work as a teacher more. Then he thought of taking old, unused material apart and rebuilding it into new songs. The record was released in June 1994 on Scat Records.

The recording was done not in a studio but on simple equipment in garages and basements, in three days. That led to mistakes: in Hardcore UFO's the guitar drops out for a moment. The band came to like the sound precisely for that. The music draws its influence from British beat, punk and psychedelia, with surrealist lyrics. After this record the group grew into one of the best-known names in lo-fi. Other labels showed interest.
werk/guided-by-voices-bee-thousand.listen: Listen to You're Not an Airplane, the closing track: notice the piano and how bare and homely the recording sounds.

werk/guided-by-voices-devil-between-my-t.text:
Devil Between My Toes is the debut of the indie rock band Guided by Voices. After the lukewarm reception of their first release in 1986 and the poor sales, the group stopped playing live and became a studio band. Steve Wilbur recorded most of the songs in his eight-track studio, and a few songs came about in Robert Pollard's basement. The record was self-funded and came out in an edition of 300 copies.

The sleeve shows Pollard's rooster Big Daddy, photographed by Mitch Mitchell through a fence. The sound has been described as post-punk with influences from R.E.M. In A Portrait Destroyed by Fire the guitar sounds like a farewell song, while Discussing Wallace Chambers is lighter and foreshadows something of the later sound.
werk/guided-by-voices-devil-between-my-t.listen: Listen to A Portrait Destroyed by Fire and notice how the guitar carries the song.

werk/guided-by-voices-same-place-the-fly.text:
Same Place the Fly Got Smashed is Guided by Voices' fourth album and continues the beginning of the band's lo-fi period. The production sounds clearly less clear and sharp than on the earlier records. Robert Pollard calls it a concept album with a continuous story about an alcoholic who commits a murder and is ultimately executed for it.

Airshow '88 begins with a spoken fragment from the 1990 television film Shattered Dreams. Pollard counts this album among his best work and calls the lyrics of Pendulum the finest he ever wrote. Alongside him, Jim Pollard plays guitar, Greg Demos bass and Don Thrasher drums.
werk/guided-by-voices-same-place-the-fly.listen: Listen to Pendulum, a song of less than two minutes, and notice the lyrics, which Pollard himself calls his favourite.

werk/guided-by-voices-sandbox.text:
Sandbox is Guided by Voices' second studio album, from 1987. It has twelve short songs, most of about two minutes. In 1995 Robert Pollard described it as an attempt to make an enormous power pop record for less than a thousand dollars. Steve Wilbur plays guitar on Barricade and Can't Stop.

The reception was divided. AllMusic gave two out of five stars and felt that the band was taking a step back. Byron Coley of Spin, on the other hand, called the group one of the sharpest-sounding Anglophile pop bands in the Midwest since Green. In Spin's 1995 guide the record received just a 1 out of 10.
werk/guided-by-voices-sandbox.listen: Listen to A Visit to the Creep Doctor, a song of under two minutes, and notice how short and direct it is.

werk/guided-by-voices-self-inflicted-aer.text:
After earlier records that failed commercially, the band's budget shrank considerably. Guided by Voices' third album was therefore released at their own expense, in an edition of 500 copies. It was recorded at Steve Wilbur's home, on an eight-track recorder.

That limited recording technique produced something that would remain a hallmark of the group: a lo-fi sound. Many people therefore see this album as the first record with the band's true trademark. It is also the only album on which the drummer Bruce Smith plays. The fourteen pieces are mostly short. Dying to Try This lasts a little over a minute and Liar's Tale under two minutes, while An Earful o' Wax and Radio Show (Trust the Wizard) run longer.
werk/guided-by-voices-self-inflicted-aer.listen: Listen to Dying to Try This and notice how short and rough this song sounds, recorded with few means.

werk/guns-n-roses-appetite-for-destructi.text:
Guns N' Roses formed in 1985, played often in the clubs of Los Angeles and signed with Geffen in March 1986. In January 1987 the recording began at Rumbo Recorders under the producer Mike Clink, who was chosen after several other candidates. The budget was about 370,000 dollars. Slash searched for a long time for his guitar sound, and Axl Rose recorded his vocals line by line.

The songs come from the band's daily life. Welcome To The Jungle is partly about an encounter Rose had in New York, Mr. Brownstone about the band's heroin problems and Out Ta Get Me about Rose's youth in Indiana. The album at first received little attention and became a success only a year later, after tours and heavy radio play for Welcome To The Jungle, Paradise City and Sweet Child O' Mine. Critics at first responded in mixed fashion and now hail it as one of the best hard rock albums of the 1980s.
werk/guns-n-roses-appetite-for-destructi.listen: In Sweet Child O' Mine, listen to Slash's guitar work. Notice how the guitar and the vocals alternate.

werk/hank-jones-here-s-love.text:
In 1963 the pianist Hank Jones recorded an album for the Argo label with arrangements of the music from Here's Love, Meredith Willson's Broadway musical. The musical is based on the film Miracle on 34th Street. All ten pieces are by Willson, including Here's Love, My Wish, Dear Mister Santa Claus and Pine Cones and Holly Berries.

Jones plays in a quartet with the guitarist Kenny Burrell, the bassist Milt Hinton and the drummer Elvin Jones. The pieces last from just over two to almost five minutes: Love, Come Take Me Again is the shortest, Pine Cones and Holly Berries the longest. Allmusic gave the record three stars.
werk/hank-jones-here-s-love.listen: Listen to Dear Mister Santa Claus and notice how the quartet takes a song from a musical as a starting point for jazz.

werk/hank-jones-porgy-and-bess.text:
Porgy And Bess, subtitled Swingin' Impressions, contains interpretations of music from George Gershwin's opera. The pianist Hank Jones recorded the album in 1958 for Capitol. He is accompanied by the guitarist Kenny Burrell, the bassist Milt Hinton and his brother Elvin Jones on drums and percussion. All the pieces come from the opera, from Summertime to I Ain't Got No Shame.

The reviews were divided. AllMusic gave three stars. On All About Jazz, Franz Matzner noticed the almost minimalist piano playing and Elvin's light touch, which result in a modest, intimate production. In JazzTimes, Thomas Conrad was less enthusiastic: according to him, the renditions of Summertime and It Ain't Necessarily So offer no important insights, although he calls them stylised and impeccable.
werk/hank-jones-porgy-and-bess.listen: Listen to Summertime and notice how few notes the piano needs and how lightly the drums play underneath.

werk/hank-jones-the-talented-touch.text:
The Talented Touch is an album by the pianist Hank Jones, recorded in 1958 for the Capitol label. He plays in a quartet with the guitarist Barry Galbraith, the bassist Milt Hinton and the drummer Osie Johnson. The programme consists mostly of well-known songs, including by Rodgers and Hart, Jerome Kern and Cole Porter, and one original piece, Let Me Know. The pieces are short: none lasts much longer than three and a half minutes.

AllMusic gave the album three and a half stars and wrote that musicians of this calibre can say a great deal in so little time. JazzTimes praised the elegant finish and found it a pleasant, reassuring piano album to put on after a hard day's work, although the caution makes the session less essential.
werk/hank-jones-the-talented-touch.listen: Listen to My One and Only Love and notice how the pianist plays the melody straight and only adds soft, tinkling embellishments.

werk/hank-mobley-mobley-s-message.text:
Mobley's Message is an album by the tenor saxophonist Hank Mobley, recorded on 20 July 1956 and released in 1957 on the Prestige label. He plays with the trumpeter Donald Byrd, the pianist Barry Harris, the bassist Doug Watkins and the drummer Art Taylor. On one piece the alto saxophonist Jackie McLean is a guest.

The repertoire combines work by others with original compositions. Bouncing with Bud comes from Bud Powell, 52nd Street Theme from Thelonious Monk, Au Privave from Charlie Parker and Little Girl Blue from Rodgers and Hart. Minor Disturbance and Alternating Current were written by the bandleader himself. Byrd does not play on Little Girl Blue, and McLean can be heard only on Au Privave.
werk/hank-mobley-mobley-s-message.listen: In Au Privave, listen to the two saxophones: Mobley on tenor and Jackie McLean on alto, who plays only on this piece.

werk/hank-mobley-tenor-conclave.text:
Four tenor saxophonists on one record: that is Tenor Conclave. John Coltrane, Hank Mobley, Al Cohn and Zoot Sims recorded the album in 1956 for Prestige Records, which released it in early 1957. Behind them plays a rhythm section with Red Garland on piano, Paul Chambers on bass and Art Taylor on drums.

There are four long pieces on it. The title track and Bob's Boys are by one of the four saxophonists himself, and in addition they play Just You, Just Me and Irving Berlin's How Deep Is the Ocean. That last piece lasts well over fifteen minutes. In 1962 Prestige reissued the record with a different sleeve, on which Coltrane's name stood out more.
werk/hank-mobley-tenor-conclave.listen: Listen to Tenor Conclave and try to hear when one saxophonist takes over the solo from another.

werk/hank-williams-moanin-the-blues.text:
Moanin' the Blues was released in 1952 on MGM Records as the second and last studio album by the American country singer Hank Williams. There was no new music on it: the songs had been recorded between 1947 and 1951 and mostly released before. The producer Fred Rose put the record together around a blues theme. Country LPs hardly sold at the time, so the album was probably not a high priority for the label.

Unlike his debut, which consisted mostly of B-sides, this record is full of hits. Lovesick Blues, Long Gone Lonesome Blues and Honky Tonk Blues reached number one on the country chart. Moanin' the Blues and I'm a Long Gone Daddy made the top ten. I'm So Lonesome I Could Cry did not chart, but many regard it as the finest song Williams wrote. Apart from Lovesick Blues, he wrote everything himself.
werk/hank-williams-moanin-the-blues.listen: Listen to I'm So Lonesome I Could Cry and notice how the singer puts the loneliness of the title into his voice.

werk/harry-belafonte-love-is-a-gentle-th.text:
Love Is a Gentle Thing was released in 1959 on RCA Victor. The album consists of folk songs of varied moods, sung in a tender style. Two arrangers and conductors, Alan Greene and Bob Corman, divided the pieces between them. Edward Welker was the producer, David Stone Martin drew the sleeve and Paul Ackerman wrote the liner notes.

There are songs by a variety of writers, such as Times Are Gettin' Hard by Lee Hays of The Weavers and Go Away from My Window by John Jacob Niles. The album reached eighteenth place on Billboard's chart for mono albums. In March 1959 Billboard named it one of the week's winners and praised the sensitive singing. The AllMusic reviewer thought the songs by Hays and by Niles the best pieces, but found the variety limited.
werk/harry-belafonte-love-is-a-gentle-th.listen: Listen to Times Are Gettin' Hard and notice how sensitively the singer delivers the lyrics.

werk/harry-belafonte-mark-twain-and-othe.text:
Harry Belafonte made his debut album in 1954 for RCA Victor. Hugo Winterhalter supervised the orchestra and the chorus; as producers, Henri René, Jack Lewis and Joe Carlton are also named alongside him. Millard Thomas played guitar.

The album contains twelve folk songs, including Mark Twain, John Henry and Lord Randall. Many pieces are traditionals. The name Paul Campbell in the credits is fictitious: it was used so that public domain material could be registered. Leonard Feather wrote the liner notes. The record reached number 3 on the Billboard Albums Chart and stayed there for four weeks. The shortest piece, The Next Big River, lasts only twenty seconds.
werk/harry-belafonte-mark-twain-and-othe.listen: Listen to The Next Big River and notice how short a track on this record can be. Then compare it with the much longer Lord Randall.

werk/harry-belafonte-my-lord-what-a-morn.text:
My Lord What a Mornin' is an album of spirituals that RCA Victor released in 1960. Besides the lead singer, a group also sings along, The Belafonte Folk Singers. Bob Corman conducted, Bob Bollard produced and Bob Simpson was the engineer. The poet Langston Hughes wrote the liner notes.

The album features old, traditional songs such as Ezekiel, Were You There When They Crucified My Lord? and Swing Low. There are also pieces that the singer wrote with Gene Corman and Milton Okun, including Wake Up Jacob, the title song and Oh Freedom. In 1995 the album was reissued with five extra tracks, including Michael Row the Boat Ashore.
werk/harry-belafonte-my-lord-what-a-morn.listen: Listen to Swing Low and notice how the solo voice and the chorus together carry this traditional song.

werk/harry-styles-fine-line.text:
After his first solo album, Harry Styles wanted to sound more playful and adventurous. Many songs came about after the end of his relationship with the model Camille Rowe. The producer Kid Harpoon urged him to write down his feelings. Together with Tyler Johnson he recorded the album, including at the Shangri-La studio. He drew inspiration from David Bowie, Van Morrison, Paul McCartney and Joni Mitchell. Her album Blue even led him to a dulcimer, which he bought from its maker.

Fine Line is mainly a pop album with rock, psychedelia, folk, soul and funk. He wrote Golden in the studio kitchen, inspired by Van Morrison. Watermelon Sugar got its title from a novel by Richard Brautigan that was lying around in the studio. Critics were positive, especially about the production. Watermelon Sugar earned a Grammy.
werk/harry-styles-fine-line.listen: In Cherry, listen all the way to the end. There you hear the voice of his ex-girlfriend, who was speaking French on the phone during the recording.

werk/harry-styles-harry-s-house.text:
Harry Styles's third solo album came about largely in 2020 and 2021, including at the Shangri-La studio in Malibu. The title refers to Hosono House by the Japanese musician Haruomi Hosono, a record he had heard during a stay in Japan. The house of the title stands for his own head: a day full of happy and sad music. This makes it his most personal work.

The sound leans on Japanese city pop of the 1970s and 1980s, with synth-pop, new wave, pop rock and pop-funk. Music For a Sushi Restaurant was at first intended as the album title. Matilda is named after Roald Dahl's book. John Mayer plays guitar on Cinema and Daydreaming. As It Was became the biggest single. Critics were full of praise for the production, and the album won a Grammy for Album of the Year.
werk/harry-styles-harry-s-house.listen: In Music For a Sushi Restaurant, listen to the synthesizers and the rhythm. Notice how the song sounds playful and danceable at the same time.

werk/hector-lavoe-comedia.text:
Comedia is the third solo album by the Puerto Rican singer Héctor Lavoe. It came out in 1978 on Fania Records and was recorded at La Tierra Sound Studios in New York. Willie Colón produced the record and mixed almost all the tracks. The album has seven pieces, ranging from three and a half minutes to well over ten minutes.

The best-known piece is El Cantante, written by Rubén Blades. At well over ten minutes it is also the longest piece, and a violin plays on it. The album later received a great deal of recognition. In 2006 it appeared in a list of ten classic salsa records in the magazine Hispanic, and in October 2024 Rolling Stone named it one of the fifty best salsa albums of all time.
werk/hector-lavoe-comedia.listen: Listen to El Cantante, the opening track of well over ten minutes. Notice how the voice sustains for so long and which instruments sound alongside it.

werk/hector-lavoe-de-ti-depende.text:
De ti depende is Héctor Lavoe's second solo album and came out in 1976 on Fania Records. Willie Colón produced the record and also wrote a number of the arrangements. Jerry Masucci was executive producer. In the chorus, Rubén Blades and Colón himself, among others, sing along, and Yomo Toro plays guitar. The sound is salsa from New York, with trombones, trumpet, conga and bongo.

The first single, Periodico de Ayer, is regarded as one of the most popular salsa songs ever. The album has eight pieces, including Vamos a Reír un Poco, Consejo de Oro and Mentira.
werk/hector-lavoe-de-ti-depende.listen: Listen to Periódico de Ayer and notice Lavoe's singing and the horns beneath it.
